records.title: Provisional COVID-19 Mortality Surveillance
records.retrieval_query: What were the reported daily or weekly Covid-19 death counts over time in the relevant jurisdiction(s) around and before 2020-10-21, and do they show a flat trend?

passages.P4: The provisional counts for COVID-19 deaths are based on a current flow of mortality data in the National Center for Health Statistics’ National Vital Statistics System (NVSS). National provisional counts include deaths occurring within the 50 states and the District of Columbia that have been received and coded as of the date specified. It can take several weeks for death records to be submitted, processed, coded, and tabulated. Therefore, the data shown on this page may be incomplete, and will likely not include all deaths that occurred during a given time period, especially for the more recent time periods. Death counts for earlier weeks are continually revised and may increase or decrease as new and updated death certificate data are received from the states by NCHS.
passages.P5: This page highlights provisional COVID-19 mortality in the following ways: (1) display of overall deaths by week for data from 2015 through the current year, (2) weekly counts of death for COVID-19 and deaths from all causes, (3) an index of COVID-19 mortality surveillance datasets. Additionally, users can access NVSS surveillance data through the following platforms: CDC WONDER, CDC’s COVID Data Tracker, CDC’s Respiratory Virus Index, and the following figures and tables. Data for these surveillance tools are updated weekly with the most current death data received.
passages.P6: ### Deaths Attributed to COVID-19 on Death Certificates
passages.P7: ### Table 1. Provisional death counts by time period and jurisdiction, United States.
passages.P8: This table has counts of deaths involving COVID-19 and other select causes of death by time-period in which the death occurred. For data on deaths involving COVID-19 by time-period and jurisdiction, .
passages.P10: NOTE: Empty data cells represent death counts between 1-9 that have been suppressed in accordance with NCHS confidentiality standards. Number of deaths reported on this page are the total number of deaths received and coded as of the date of analysis and do not represent all deaths that occurred in that period. Data are incomplete because of the lag in time between when the death occurred and when the death certificate is completed, submitted to NCHS and processed for reporting purposes. This delay can range from 1 week to 8 weeks or more, depending on the jurisdiction and cause of death. United States death counts include the 50 states, plus the District of Columbia and New York City. New York state estimates exclude New York City.
passages.P11: [1] Deaths with confirmed or presumed COVID-19, coded to ICD–10 code U07.1.
passages.P12: [2] Percent of expected deaths is the number of deaths for all causes for these time-periods in 2020-2026 compared to the average number across the same time-period in 2017–2019. Previous analyses of 2015–2016 provisional data completeness have found that completeness is lower in the first few weeks following the date of death (<25%), and then increases over time such that data are generally at least 75% complete within 8 weeks of when the death occurred. Recent improvements in the timeliness of provisional mortality data suggest that the data are at least 94% complete within 8 weeks of when the death occurred, see Technical Notes.
passages.P13: [3] Deaths with confirmed or presumed COVID-19, pneumonia, or influenza, coded to ICD–10 codes U07.1 or J09–J18.9.

passages.P2: The GBD study is the largest and most comprehensive effort to quantify health loss across places and over time, so health systems can be improved and disparities eliminated.
passages.P3:
607 billion+
highly standardized and comprehensive estimates measure health outcomes and systems.
passages.P4:
463
health outcomes and risk factors provide a powerful basis for insights on global health trends and challenges.
passages.P5:
204
countries and territories, plus dozens of subnational locations show trends at regional, national, and local levels.
passages.P6:
20,000+
individuals from 167 countries and territories collaborate in vetting GBD data sources and estimates.
passages.P8: ## GBD Health State Survey – we need your help!
passages.P10: The GBD study estimates the health impact of hundreds of diseases and injuries in every country in the world. A key input is how people judge the severity of different health conditions, from mild hearing loss to severe depression to the aftermath of a stroke. These judgments come directly from surveys like this one, so your responses feed into the estimates used by governments, WHO, and researchers worldwide.
passages.P11: You’ll be shown short descriptions of two health conditions at a time and asked which person you consider healthier. No medical background is needed, and it is available in 12 languages. Responses are anonymous.
passages.P13: Please share the survey with anyone with an interest in global health. The more people who respond, from as many countries and backgrounds as possible, the stronger the estimates will be.
passages.P14: Thank you for your time and support.
passages.P16: The 2026 fall/winter application window is currently open, and we are accepting applications through **11:59 p.m., Pacific time on December 31, 2026**. Decisions for all applications submitted during this window will be sent to all applicants by March 31, 2027.
passages.P19: The latest global burden of diseases, injuries, and risk factors study (GBD) – an update through the year 2023 – provides a comprehensive picture of the world’s health following the COVID-19 pandemic.
